newsitem.title: DENMARK: New law forces Danish bikers out of strongholds.
newsitem.headline: New law forces Danish bikers out of strongholds.

text.p: Rival Danish bikers in the front line of a brutal Nordic gang war moved out of fortified strongholds across the country as emergency legislation suspending their right of assembly took effect on Wednesday.

The law -- which has broad political support, but worries some civil rights groups -- allows police to stop biker gang members entering their clubhouses or congregating in private homes, bars, or meeting halls until further notice.

"We are going out to the strongholds and giving them notice that they can't go in there any more," Chief Inspector Kai Vittrup, in charge of serving the orders in the capital and throughout eastern Denmark, told Reuters.

"We're going to their private homes and trying to look for them wherever they are and because some of them are in prison we're going to the prisons too, to tell them that they are not able to go back to the strongholds," he said.

Although believed to have extensive weapons caches, the feuding Hell's Angels and Bandidos gangs avoided confrontation with police, who recently ordered 200 bulletproof vests from Norway in response to spiralling biker violence.

"On each side, Hell's Angels and Bandidos, I think they have decided more or less to move out," Vittrup said, adding that Hell's Angels moved their belongings from their missile-scarred headquarters on central Copenhagen's Titangade on Tuesday night.
"Even before the law was officially announced this morning we could see movement from Titangade and other strongholds in the Copenhagen area. We are quite satisfied with that," he said.

The law was announced two weeks ago as the first step in a planned government package of legislation to quash a vicious turf war which in almost three years has killed seven people and wounded many more in Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden.

The government offensive took on new urgency on October 6 when, in the bloodiest incident yet, attackers fired an anti-tank missile into a mass of party-goers at the Titangade clubhouse, killing two and wounding 19.
The raid increased demands for action from frightened Danes living near biker clubs, which have been the targets of bomb, grenade, machine gun and missile attacks.
Provincial police on Wednesday reported Hell's Angels and allied gangs vacating buildings in Aarhus, Denmark's second city, and in the north Jutland port of Aalborg.
The Bandidos were said to be evacuating their headquarters at Stenloese, west of Copenhagen, and at least two other locations.
The new law has raised the possibility that local authorities may have to rehouse, at public expense, bikers made homeless by the ban.
Stenloese Mayor Johannes Nielsen said that five persons were registered as permanent residents of the Bandidos complex there.
"If they apply to the council, according to the welfare law we must ensure that they have a bed to sleep in," he said.
Nielsen, however, added that his rural district had no vacant accommodation and Bandido applicants "might have to be rehoused far away from here".

Some security analysts are sceptical that driving the combatants underground will end the war, but Justice Minister Bjoern Westh has said that this bill is only the first step and measures to give police tougher gang-busting powers will follow.
Danish journalist Ambro Kragh has covered the biker story for the past six years.

He believes that in the face of an external threat, such as a possible blanket ban on Hell's Angels and Bandidos, the two gangs might stop fighting in order not to provoke a reaction that might destroy them both.

"As the so-called one percent of motorcyclists who are criminals, they have a sense of brotherhood among themselves and I believe they are going to meet and say: "Look, we are going to be killed by the politicians if we continue (fighting)'," Kragh told Reuters.
